https://www.dealstreetasia.com/stories/s.text: China's Sinochem sells 14% Pirelli stake to Czech billionaire Michal Strnad Czech billionaire Michal Strnad, chairman and owner of Ammunition and arms maker Czechoslovak Group (CSG), arrives at Euronext Amsterdam in Amsterdam, Netherlands, January 23, 2026. REUTERS/Piroschka van de Wouw 31 July, 2026 Sinochem has sold a 14% stake in Pirelli to Czech billionaire Michal Strnad, the two parties said on Thursday, with the Chinese state-owned group significantly scaling back its investment in the Italian tyremaker. Sinochem said it had sold the shares, part of its overall 34.1% shareholding through a block-trade deal, cutting its stake to 20.1%, this becoming Pirelli’s second largest investor. In a separate statement, Strnad’s investment company Lumina Crown said it had acquired the 14% stake, becoming Pirelli’s third largest shareholder and aiming for a “long-term investment” in the company. Strnad is the controlling shareholder of defence and industrial group Czechoslovak Group (CSG). According to data reported on the Italian stock exchange website, the shares were sold at €6.50 each, valuing the 14% stake at around €987 million ($1.14 billion). Pirelli shares closed at 6.51 euros on Thursday. The sale draws a line under years of tensions between Pirelli’s main investors following Italy’s moves to curb Sinochem’s influence at the company. As a consequence of the deal, Camfin – the vehicle of Executive Chairman Marco Tronchetti Provera, the Italian businessman who has led the Milan-based tyre maker for more than three decades – becomes Pirelli’s largest shareholder with a 26% stake. Sinochem’s influence over the company has been sharply curtailed since the Italian government intervened twice, in 2023 and earlier this year, using its so-called “golden power” rules to protect strategic assets. Under more recent restrictions imposed by Rome, Sinochem got just three representatives on Pirelli’s 15-member board, which is effectively controlled by Camfin. Its appointees are also barred from holding key executive positions such as chairman or chief executive. Sinochem was advised in the deal by BNP Paribas; Lumina Crown was advised by Jefferies. (Image: Getty) Experts are calling on health chiefs to reveal where contaminated eggs linked to a deadly salmonella outbreak in the UK were imported from. Officials have confirmed that imported eggs are being investigated as a potential source of the outbreak, which has affected more than 200 people across the UK and been linked to one death. However, the country the eggs came from has not been publicly identified, prompting calls for greater transparency over their origin. "If necessary, restrictions should be imposed on importations." So far, 199 cases have been confirmed in England, alongside six in Scotland, one in Wales and one in Northern Ireland. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT M5 traffic LIVE: Delays as all traffic stopped at J6 after horror crash Homes in 44 UK areas told ‘prepare to turn off gas, water and electricity’ The strain behind the outbreak has been identified as Salmonella Enteritidis, which is commonly associated with poultry and eggs. Officials have identified five unnamed food businesses which were visited by two or more people who later became ill. Those affected are understood to have eaten at cafes and restaurants. Concerns over imported eggs had already been raised before the outbreak. Earlier this year, the British Egg Industry Council warned of "significant" potential risks associated with increasing egg imports. Its Shell Shocked report said UK imports had increased by 600 million eggs since 2021, with growth largely driven by supplies from Ukraine and Poland. However, neither country has been identified as the source of the current UK outbreak. Nick Allen, chief executive of the BEIC, said: "It is deeply concerning that imported eggs are once again under scrutiny in connection with a serious Salmonella outbreak. "We have repeatedly raised concerns about the risks associated with imported eggs and egg products with Government, most recently through our Shell Shocked report." Kevin Coles, of the British Egg Information Service, also argued consumers should be told where eggs have originated. He said: "We have been urging the Government to protect British consumers by banning imported eggs for a while. "But in the meantime, you can check if your eggs are British by looking for the British Lion mark." The Food Standards Agency (FSA) stressed that investigators have not yet established the exact cause of the outbreak. Jacquelyn McCormick, Head of Incidents at the FSA, said: "The exact cause has not yet been identified, however investigations so far have identified links to eggs imported from outside the UK, mainly used by food service and catering establishments such as restaurants or cafes, as a potential source. "There is no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected." She added that properly cooked and hygienically handled eggs should not present a food safety risk. A separate salmonella outbreak linked to eggs is currently being investigated in Belgium, where around 300 people are reported to have fallen ill. Eggs involved there were reportedly distributed to several European countries, including Poland, although the UK has not been listed among them. https://www.ecoportal.net/en/pound-robot.text: Technology An Ontario 15 year old student built a bionic turtle that swims on flippers instead of propellers, and in his grandparents’ backyard pool it read replicated coral bleaching correctly 96 times out of 100 By Hugo Rojas AUG 26, 2026 5:50 PM 5 MIN READ Credits: Canadian high school student with bionic turtle Stay in the loop Follow us on Google News → The machine sits on the wet coping with water still running off it. Four printed flippers, a clear tube of electronics, a camera the size of a thumb . It weighs eleven pounds, roughly a large house cat . What the robot turtle did on the way across the pool matters more than any of that. It went from one end to the other without stirring the water , and that single property is the reason the thing exists at all. What a flipper does that a propeller cannot A propeller moves a vehicle by throwing water backward. The turbulence is not a side effect of the propulsion. It is the propulsion , and the noise comes with it. Over a shipwreck that costs nothing. Over a reef in trouble it costs a great deal, because the instrument starts damaging the thing it came to measure, lifting sediment, scattering animals and putting pressurized water across structures that break easily. A turtle solves the same problem with a different motion. The front pair of limbs row it forward while the back pair steer, and the wake it leaves is something reef animals live with already. That split is copied directly, two large flippers at the front for thrust and two smaller ones behind for stability and direction. The builder put the reasoning plainly. Related Energy Two underwater “dragons” are being turned into whale listeners in the Faroe Islands before dozens more tidal kites are allowed to fly through the fjords Climate The Great Lakes are entering the weeks when warm water can spin up tornado-shaped funnels beneath ordinary fall clouds, and some disappear again within 20 minutes He did not want, he told an American magazine, to harm the places he was hoping to protect. What is inside the shell The brain is a hobby computer the size of a credit card, the same board sold for classrooms and garage projects, sealed inside a clear acrylic tube. It runs the detection models, logs what it sees and sends it out wirelessly. A location module lets it follow a preset grid on its own, which removes the tether that most survey machines drag behind them. The sensing is more crowded than it looks. A camera in the nose, lights for dark water, an ultrasonic transducer that finds obstacles by sound, depth sensors, and a homemade holographic imager for particles too small to photograph. Motorized fins handle buoyancy. A lithium battery gives about eight hours, a solar panel stretches that, and the whole thing cruises at half a mile an hour, which is not coincidentally the speed of a turtle . The pool, and what the 96 percent measured Almost all of the testing happened in a grandparents’ backyard pool a little over eight feet deep. He printed a reef simulator, put it on the bottom and taught the machine what bleaching and invasive growth look like. Under those conditions it flagged replicated bleaching correctly 96 percent of the time. Then it went into Lake Ontario, which is nothing like a pool. Murk, current and shifting light are what forced the front lights and the sound based obstacle finder onto the design, and none of that was in the original drawing. The work took the national innovation prize at the Canadian science fair in Fredericton, then went to the European young scientists contest in Riga. It came home with one of the four first prizes , worth around 8,000 dollars, from a field the organizers counted at 133 entrants representing 37 countries. That number came out of chlorinated water at a fixed depth under steady light, scoring printed models whose appearance the machine had been shown in advance. A reef is none of those things . It is cold, murky, moving, and its bleaching does not come off a printer. Depth is capped by the acrylic housing and the pressure ratings of what is inside it, so the real ceiling is unknown until somebody goes and finds it. Telling a real signal from a lookalike in open water is its own discipline, the same problem as a sensor learning to separate a whale from a drifting ghost net beneath a floating turbine. The next step is other environments, which is exactly what separates a prototype from an instrument . What the price tag actually changes The interesting thing about that computer is how ordinary it is . It is not specialist hardware and it does not want a support vessel, and reef monitoring has historically wanted both. Everything else came off a home printer and a parts shelf, which puts the build inside a school budget rather than a research grant. Cheap gear doing expensive work has a track record in this field, including the homemade torpedo that carried living coral 217 feet down so divers could start new colonies with it. He wants to add water sampling next, he told the organizers , and the prize money is going toward it. The pool is finished with. The ocean has not started . Read the whole thing? https://www.rte.ie/news/world/2026/0922/.text: Updated / Tuesday, 22 Sep 2026 19:46 Getty Ukrainian firefighters pictured working at a destroyed warehouse in Russian strikes on Kyiv Russian missiles and drones struck at least four Ukrainian regions overnight, killing five people, officials said have said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country's forces had damaged two more Russian oil refineries in their latest long-range strikes. The continuing exchange of aerial attacks, even as front-line positions remain largely unchanged, provided the backdrop for Mr Zelensky's visit to the US. US President Donald Trump has called on Mr Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are contributing to global shortages and higher prices. The supply crunch has also been aggravated by reduced oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz following the outbreak of the Iran war. Ukraine began attacking Russian refineries after Russia repeatedly targeted Ukraine's power grid. Mr Zelensky has offered to halt Ukraine's attacks if Russia ends its strikes on energy infrastructure. Mr Zelensky was scheduled to meet Mr Trump and other world leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York. He is seeking their help to end Russia's more than four-and-a-half-year-old invasion. Russia's President Vladimir Putin is not due to attend the annual event. A rescuer uses an aerial work platform to extinguish a fire at Zaporizhzhia National University The war, which Western officials claim has killed more than 500,000 Russian troops, has had global repercussions. Western analysts estimate that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Mr Zelensky also wants help to ensure the flow of Ukrainian grain and other farm products to world markets through the Black Sea. Russian strikes on cargo vessels have severely disrupted Ukraine's exports, hurting its economy and threatening global supplies. Russia and Ukraine have in recent years accounted for around 30% of the world's wheat exports and 12% of corn exports, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. However last month, attacks slashed both countries' agricultural exports by two-thirds, Thomas de Waal of the Brussels-based think tank Carnegie Europe said in a report. "The lack of that grain in world markets puts several African countries at risk of famine, while world cereal prices, already pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, could rise even higher," he said. Mr Zelensky began his visit to New York by meeting with US senators. He thanked them for what he described as strong bipartisan support for Ukraine and for backing a tougher sanctions bill against Russia that Mr Trump signed into law. France's President Emmanuel Macron meets with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky Peace and security would be closer once the legislation was fully implemented, Mr Zelensky said. He said on social media that he had briefed senators on de-escalation proposals he planned to discuss with Mr Trump. Mr Zelensky also planned to press Mr Trump for more US-made Patriot air defence systems, which Ukraine said it urgently needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Mr Zelensky said that Ukrainian special forces struck the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, south-east of Moscow, and another refinery in the neighbouring Bashkortostan region in overnight attacks. One person was killed and four others were wounded in the Samara attack, regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said. He said that "the enemy targeted industrial facilities" but did not specify which ones. The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces downed 297 Ukrainian drones over 14 Russian regions overnight, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula. Russia's overnight strike on Ukraine included anti-ship missiles, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and more than 200 drones, Ukraine's air force said. The strikes killed four people in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration. A drone also killed a woman in the northern Sumy region, local police said. The strikes across Ukrainian regions damaged homes, businesses and storage facilities, wounding at least five people, authorities said. Five people were wounded in the capital, Kyiv, according to officials. The Russian Defence Ministry said that its forces struck metallurgical and chemical industries, the fuel and energy sector, and the military-industrial complex, as well as port infrastructure facilities in four regions of Ukraine. They included a Fire Point plant in Kyiv producing components for long-range cruise missiles and a tobacco factory in the central Poltava region used to make small arms ammunition, it said.
